claim: Quickly and accurately extracting information about a touched object's orientation is a critical aspect of dexterous object manipulation.
source: Quickly and accurately extracting information about a touched object's orientation is a critical aspect of dexterous object manipulation.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of tactile orientation processing in manipulation, presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The speed and acuity of tactile edge orientation processing with respect to the fingertips as reported in previous perceptual studies appear inadequate for dexterous manipulation.
source: However, the speed and acuity of tactile edge orientation processing with respect to the fingertips as reported in previous perceptual studies appear inadequate in these respects.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous perceptual studies and comparison to manipulation requirements.

claim: Participants extracted tactile information about edge orientation within 200 ms of first touching the object.
source: Participants extracted tactile information about edge orientation very quickly, using it within 200 ms of first touching the object.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements of rotation onset time reported in the study.

claim: With edges spanning the entire fingertip, edge-orientation resolution was better than 3° in the object manipulation task.
source: With edges spanning the entire fingertip, edge-orientation resolution was better than 3° in our object manipulation task, which is several times better than reported in previous perceptual studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the pointer-alignment task with infinite edge length.

claim: Edge-orientation resolution in the manipulation task is several times better than reported in previous perceptual studies.
source: With edges spanning the entire fingertip, edge-orientation resolution was better than 3° in our object manipulation task, which is several times better than reported in previous perceptual studies.
evidence: This claim compares the current experimental results to previously published perceptual studies.

claim: Performance remained impressive even with edges as short as 2 mm.
source: Performance remained impressive even with edges as short as 2 mm, consistent with our ability to precisely manipulate very small objects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing alignment accuracy with 2 mm edges.

claim: Fingertip numbness due to events like cold exposure and nerve injury can degrade or even preclude fine manual dexterity.
source: Indeed, fingertip numbness due to events like cold exposure and nerve injury can degrade or even preclude fine manual dexterity (Moberg, 1958; Chemnitz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on the effects of fingertip numbness.

claim: For edges that span a large portion of the fingertip, the reported perceptual orientation acuity is 10–20°.
source: However, perceptual studies of tactile edge orientation have been done (Lechelt, 1992; Bensmaia et al., 2008; Peters et al., 2015), and for edges that span a large portion of the fingertip, the reported orientation acuity is 10–20°.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous perceptual studies.

claim: For shorter edges (2 mm long), the reported perceptual orientation acuity is around 90°.
source: For shorter edges, which only engage a small part of the fingertip, as is typical during fine manipulation tasks like buttoning, the reported perceptual orientation acuity is even cruder, around 90° for a 2 mm long edge (Peters et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous perceptual study.

claim: Participants were within 3° of the target orientation for edges spanning the entire contact area of the fingertip.
source: On average, participants were within 3° of the target orientation for edges spanning the entire contact area of the fingertip, similar to their performance in a visually-guided version of the same task, and considerably better than the acuity of edge orientation processing previously reported in studies of tactile perception (Lechelt, 1992; Bensmaia et al., 2008; Peters et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from the main experiment.

claim: Tactile performance with infinite edges was similar to performance in a visually-guided version of the same task.
source: On average, participants were within 3° of the target orientation for edges spanning the entire contact area of the fingertip, similar to their performance in a visually-guided version of the same task, and considerably better than the acuity of edge orientation processing previously reported in studies of tactile perception (Lechelt, 1992; Bensmaia et al., 2008; Peters et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data from tactile and visual conditions.

claim: Participants oriented the unseen dial to within 11° of the target orientation for a 2 mm long edge.
source: Performance remained impressive even with much shorter edges, with participants orienting the unseen dial to within 11° of the target orientation for a 2 mm long edge.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from the 2 mm edge condition.

claim: Participants initiated appropriate dial rotation within ~200 ms of initially touching the edge.
source: We also found that participants gathered and processed the relevant tactile information quickly, initiating appropriate dial rotation within ~200 ms of initially touching the edge.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of rotation onset time.

claim: First-order tactile neurons branch in the fingertip skin.
source: Based on a simple model, we propose that this exquisite capacity may reflect a previously largely overlooked feature of the peripheral tactile apparatus (Friedman et al., 2002; Dodson et al., 1998; Wheat et al., 1995; Saal et al., 2017) – namely, that first-order tactile neurons branch in the fingertip skin (Cauna, 1956; Cauna, 1959; Nolano et al., 2003) and have cutaneous receptive fields with multiple highly-sensitive zones (or 'subfields') (Johansson, 1978; Phillips et al., 1992; Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014; Suresh et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: First-order tactile neurons have cutaneous receptive fields with multiple highly-sensitive zones (or 'subfields').
source: Based on a simple model, we propose that this exquisite capacity may reflect a previously largely overlooked feature of the peripheral tactile apparatus (Friedman et al., 2002; Dodson et al., 1998; Wheat et al., 1995; Saal et al., 2017) – namely, that first-order tactile neurons branch in the fingertip skin (Cauna, 1956; Cauna, 1959; Nolano et al., 2003) and have cutaneous receptive fields with multiple highly-sensitive zones (or 'subfields') (Johansson, 1978; Phillips et al., 1992; Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014; Suresh et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous neurophysiological studies.

claim: Edge length significantly affected the absolute alignment error.
source: Edge length significantly affected the absolute alignment error (F5,45 = 238.5, p<10−6), which gradually decreased with increasing length.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: With the infinite edge, the alignment error was 2.9 ± 0.5°.
source: With the infinite edge, the error was 2.9 ± 0.5° (mean ±1 SD across participants) and with the 2 mm edge it was 11.1 ± 2.9°, which was about one half of the error with the raised dot (i.e., 0 mm edge length) representing chance performance.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements.

claim: With the 2 mm edge, the alignment error was 11.1 ± 2.9°.
source: With the infinite edge, the error was 2.9 ± 0.5° (mean ±1 SD across participants) and with the 2 mm edge it was 11.1 ± 2.9°, which was about one half of the error with the raised dot (i.e., 0 mm edge length) representing chance performance.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements.

claim: Participants more frequently rotated the dial in the wrong direction with shorter edges.
source: One reason that alignment error increased with shorter edges was that participants more frequently rotated the dial in the wrong direction (F5,45 = 258.4; p<10−6).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The proportion of movements in the correct direction gradually decreased from nearly 100% with the infinite edge down to chance performance (~50%) with the raised dot.
source: The proportion of movements in the correct direction gradually decreased from nearly 100% with the infinite edge down to chance performance (~50%) with the raised dot (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: If 75% correct responses define threshold performance, the average threshold of edge length for correct rotation direction was around 2 mm.
source: If 75% correct responses define threshold performance, as is common in two alternative forced choice (2AFC) tasks, the average threshold of edge length for correct rotation direction was around 2 mm.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data using a standard psychophysical criterion.

claim: The scaling of pointer displacement based on the initial dial orientation became poorer for trials in the correct direction with shorter edges.
source: Another reason for the increased alignment error with shorter edges was that the scaling of pointer displacement based on the initial dial orientation became poorer for trials in the correct direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of experimental data on pointer displacement.

claim: With the infinite edge, participants appropriately scaled pointer displacements such that the alignment error was, on average, close to zero for each initial orientation.
source: With the infinite edge, participants appropriately scaled pointer displacements in the sense that the alignment error was, on average, close to zero for each initial orientation (top panel in Figure 2e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: There was a tendency to undershoot the target with the ±30° initial orientations and overshoot the target with ±10° initial orientations.
source: However, there was a tendency to undershoot the target with the ±30° initial orientations and overshoot the target with ±10° initial orientations.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data on pointer displacement patterns.

claim: There was a significant interaction between edge length and initial orientation on the displacement in the correct direction.
source: Indeed, there was a significant interaction between edge length and initial orientation (F25,225 = 21.1; p<10−6) together with main effects of edge length (F5,45 = 14.1; p<10−6) and initial orientation (F5,45 = 77.5; p<10−6) on the displacement in the correct direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In a follow-up experiment with 50 initial dial orientations, the absolute alignment (2.7 ± 0.4°) did not differ significantly from that recorded in the main experiment (2.9 ± 0.5°).
source: Second, in a follow-up experiment performed with the infinite edge and involving 50 rather than six initial dial orientations (see Materials and methods), the absolute alignment (2.7 ± 0.4°; mean ±1 SD across participants) did not differ significantly from that recorded in the main experiment (2.9 ± 0.5°; F1,18 = 1.19; p=0.29).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from a follow-up experiment and statistical comparison.

claim: Tactile information about edge orientation could effectively guide manipulation for edges that were 2 mm and longer.
source: Taken together, we found that tactile information about edge orientation could effectively guide manipulation for edges that were 2 mm and longer and, with an edge of infinite length relative to the fingertip, alignment accuracy was, on average, better than 3°.
evidence: This claim summarizes experimental findings from the main experiment.

claim: The time between initial contact with the dial and the onset of the rotation was 0.20 ± 0.02 s.
source: Averaged across participants' medians, the time between touch and rotation onset was 0.20 ± 0.02 s (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Rotation onset typically occurred while the contact force was still increasing towards its plateau-like state.
source: Rotation onset typically occurred while the contact force was still increasing towards its plateau-like state (Figures 1b and 3b), which, on average, was reached 0.31 ± 0.09 s after initial contact with the dial.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1b and 3b.

claim: The contact force at rotation onset (1.15 ± 0.44 N) was typically smaller than the plateau force (1.64 ± 0.83 N).
source: Accordingly, the contact force at rotation onset (1.15 ± 0.44 N, Figure 3c) was typically smaller than the plateau force (1.64 ± 0.83 N, Figure 3d; F1,9 = 11.5; p=0.008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Edge length and initial dial orientation showed no statistically significant effect on rotation onset time, time to plateau force, contact force at rotation onset, or plateau contact force.
source: Edge length and initial dial orientation showed no statistically significant effect on any of these measures.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The duration of dial rotation tended to increase with the required rotation amplitude.
source: The duration of dial rotation tended to increase with the required rotation amplitude but the size of this effect depended on the edge length.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data on rotation duration.

claim: Shorter edges that yielded smaller pointer displacements also yielded shorter rotation durations.
source: Shorter edges that yielded smaller pointer displacements also yielded shorter rotation durations (Figure 3e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: None of the participants showed a significant relationship between the absolute alignment error and the rotation onset time.
source: None of the participants showed a significant relationship between the absolute alignment error and the rotation onset time (0.01 < F1,399<3.86; 0.05 < P < 0.93, uncorrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis (ANCOVA) of experimental data.

claim: None of the participants showed a significant relationship between rotation duration and absolute alignment error.
source: In a corresponding analysis, we found that none of the participants showed a significant relationship between rotation duration and absolute alignment error (0.07 < F1,399<3.41; 0.07 < Puncorrected < 0.79).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no reliable effect of the whole trial duration on absolute alignment error.
source: Likewise, we found no reliable effect of the whole trial duration (that is, the entire time from touch to the end of the rotation) on absolute alignment error (0.01 < F1,399<6.17; 0.01 < Puncorrected < 0.92).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Sub-movements were found in 44% of all trials.
source: We found sub-movements in 44% of all trials.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by analysis of experimental data.

claim: The frequency distribution of trials with and without sub-movements was similar for all edge lengths.
source: The frequency distribution of trials with and without sub-movements was similar for all edge lengths (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) and trials with sub-movements were present in all participants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: There was no significant effect of sub-movements on the absolute alignment error or on the proportion of rotations in the correct direction.
source: Repeated measures ANOVAs with edge length, initial dial orientation, and presence of sub-movements as factors failed, however, to indicate a significant effect of sub-movements on the absolute alignment error (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e) or on the proportion of rotations in the correct direction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Study participants generated the dial rotation action based on tactile information extracted and processed essentially within ~200 ms of initial contact.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that study participants generated the dial rotation action based on tactile information extracted and processed essentially within ~200 ms of initial contact.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on multiple experimental findings about rotation onset time and lack of relationship between timing and accuracy.

claim: Alignment performance was marginally better in the visual than in the tactile condition.
source: Alignment performance was marginally better in the visual than in the tactile condition (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data from visual and tactile conditions.

claim: The absolute alignment in the visual condition (2.1 ± 0.5°) was smaller than in the tactile condition (2.9 ± 0.5°).
source: The smaller absolute alignment in the visual condition (2.1 ± 0.5°) than in the tactile condition (2.9 ± 0.5°; F1,9 = 12.9, p=0.006) mainly stemmed from smaller errors in the visual trials with initial dial orientations closest to the 0˚ target (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: The rotation onset time in the visual condition (0.07 ± 0.04 s) was shorter than in the tactile condition (0.20 ± 0.02 s).
source: The rotation onset time in the visual condition (0.07 ± 0.04 s) was shorter than in the in tactile condition (0.20 ± 0.02 s; F1,9 = 201.5, p<10−6) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), presumably because participants could program the movement based on visual information obtained before touching the dial.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: The time from touch until contact force reached its plateau was modestly shorter in the visual condition (0.25 ± 0.10 s) compared to the tactile condition (0.31 ± 0.10 s).
source: The time from touch until contact force reached its plateau was modestly shorter in the visual condition (0.25 ± 0.10 s as compared to 0.31 ± 0.10 s; F1,9 = 16.8, p=0.003; Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: For all participants in the visual condition, the onset of the rotation occurred during contact force increase.
source: Nevertheless, for all participants in the visual condition the onset of the rotation occurred during contact force increase.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data from the visual condition.

claim: The sensory condition did not significantly influence the contact force at rotation onset or the plateau force.
source: In fact, the sensory condition did not significantly influence the contact force at rotation onset or the plateau force (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d,e), and there were no statistically significant effects related to initial dial orientation on these timing and contact force parameters.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data comparing visual and tactile conditions.

claim: The kinematic structure of the rotation movement was remarkably similar in the visual and tactile pointer-alignment trials.
source: The kinematic structure of the rotation movement was remarkably similar in the visual and tactile pointer-alignment trials.
evidence: This claim summarizes multiple comparisons of kinematic measures between visual and tactile conditions.

claim: There was no statistically significant effect of sensory condition on rotation duration.
source: First, we found no statistically significant effect of sensory condition on rotation duration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the visual condition, none of the participants showed a significant effect of rotation onset time or duration of pointer rotation on alignment error.
source: Second, as for the tactile condition, in the visual condition none of the participants showed a significant effect of rotation onset time (0.011 < F1,100<3.72; 0.06 < Puncorrected < 0.92) or on the duration of the pointer rotation (0.002 < F1,100<2.47; 0.12 < Puncorrected < 0.96) on alignment error.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data from the visual condition.

claim: The frequency distribution of sub-movements did not significantly differ between the visual and tactile conditions.
source: Third, the frequency distribution of sub-movements did not significantly differ between the visual and tactile conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g,h).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The comparison of the tactile and the visual pointer-alignment trials revealed similar dial orientation accuracy and kinematics.
source: Taken together, the comparison of the tactile and the visual pointer-alignment trials revealed similar dial orientation accuracy and kinematics.
evidence: This claim summarizes multiple comparisons between visual and tactile conditions.

claim: The prevailing model supporting tactile acuity suggests that spatial details of touched objects are resolved based on the relative discharge rates of first-order tactile neurons having partly overlapping receptive fields and Gaussian-like sensitivity profiles.
source: The prevailing model supporting tactile acuity at the level we report above suggests that the spatial details of touched objects are resolved based on the relative discharge rates of first-order tactile neurons having partly overlapping receptive fields and Gaussian-like sensitivity profiles (Friedman et al., 2002; Dodson et al., 1998; Wheat et al., 1995; Saal et al., 2017; Loomis and Collins, 1978; Khalsa et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim describes the prevailing model in the field, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: First-order tactile neurons branch in the glabrous skin of the hand and innervate many spatially segregated mechanoreceptive transduction sites.
source: Here, we propose an alternative explanation based on a generally overlooked feature of the peripheral apparatus – namely, that first order tactile neurons branch in the glabrous skin of the hand and innervate many spatially segregated mechanoreceptive transduction sites (Cauna, 1956; Cauna, 1959; Nolano et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: This arrangement yields first-order tactile neurons with heterogeneous cutaneous receptive fields that include many highly sensitive zones or 'subfields', apparently randomly distributed within a circular or elliptical area typically covering five to ten papillary ridges.
source: This arrangement yields first-order tactile neurons with heterogeneous cutaneous receptive fields that include many highly sensitive zones or 'subfields', apparently randomly distributed within a circular or elliptical area typically covering five to ten papillary ridges (Johansson, 1978; Phillips et al., 1992; Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous neurophysiological studies.

claim: At the neuronal population level, the high degree of receptive field overlap in the fingertips implies that first-order tactile neuron subfields are highly intermingled.
source: At the neuronal population level, the high degree of receptive field overlap in the fingertips implies that first-order tactile neuron subfields are highly intermingled (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on known receptive field properties, illustrated in Figure 5a.

claim: For edge orientation processing, an edge contacting the skin at a certain location and orientation will primarily excite that subset of the neurons whose subfields spatially coincide with the edge.
source: Thus, for edge orientation processing, an edge contacting the skin at a certain location and orientation will primarily excite that subset of the neurons whose subfields spatially coincide with the edge, while a different subset of neurons will be primarily excited for a slightly different edge orientation (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is a theoretical proposal based on the subfield model, illustrated in Figure 5b.

claim: A coincidence code could enable the requisite edge orientation acuity and would operate at a speed suitable for the control of manipulation.
source: Such a coincidence code is attractive because it could enable the requisite edge orientation acuity and would operate at a speed suitable for the control of manipulation (Johansson and Birznieks, 2004).
evidence: This claim is a theoretical proposal supported by citation to previous work on coincidence coding.

claim: The model with subfields performed at levels slightly better than human participants, showing discrimination thresholds 1.3° for the infinite length edge to 13.1° for the 1 mm long edge.
source: First, the model with subfields performed at levels slightly better than our human participants – showing discrimination thresholds 1.3° for the infinite length edge to 13.1° for the 1 mm long edge.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results of the computational model presented in the study.

claim: The model with subfields always outperformed the model with a uniform receptive field.
source: Second, the model with subfields always outperformed the model with a uniform receptive field.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of two versions of the computational model.

claim: The performance gap between the two models grew for shorter edges (infinite edge difference = 6.4°; 1 mm = 28.4°).
source: Third, and perhaps most interestingly, the performance gap between the two models grew for shorter edges (infinite edge difference = 6.4°; 1 mm = 28.4°), suggesting that heterogeneous receptive fields are particularly beneficial for demanding tasks that utilize tactile information approaching the limits of the system's spatial resolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by results of the computational model and leads to an inference about the benefits of heterogeneous receptive fields.

claim: Heterogeneous receptive fields are particularly beneficial for demanding tasks that utilize tactile information approaching the limits of the system's spatial resolution.
source: Third, and perhaps most interestingly, the performance gap between the two models grew for shorter edges (infinite edge difference = 6.4°; 1 mm = 28.4°), suggesting that heterogeneous receptive fields are particularly beneficial for demanding tasks that utilize tactile information approaching the limits of the system's spatial resolution.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the modeling results showing greater performance differences for shorter edges.

claim: Tactile edge orientation acuity has previously been examined in perceptual discrimination and identification tasks.
source: Tactile edge orientation acuity has previously been examined in perceptual discrimination and identification tasks.
evidence: This claim refers to previous research in the field.

claim: The threshold edge-length for 75% correct rotation direction was ~2 mm, which corresponds to the dimensions of the smallest of manageable objects in everyday tasks.
source: Interestingly, the threshold edge-length for 75% correct rotation direction was ~2 mm (Figure 2d), which corresponds to the dimensions of the smallest of manageable objects in everyday tasks.
evidence: This claim connects experimental findings to real-world manipulation tasks.

claim: The dimensions of jewellery clasps or buttons designed to be as small as possible for aesthetic reasons rarely have edge lengths that go below ~2 mm.
source: For example, the dimensions of jewellery clasps or buttons designed to be as small as possible for aesthetic reasons, rarely have edge lengths that go below ~2 mm.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about the design of small manipulable objects.

claim: In all previous tasks examining edge orientation perception, the edge stimuli were externally applied to an immobilized finger.
source: Whereas participants in our pointer-alignment task actively moved their finger to contact the object, in all previous tasks examining edge orientation perception, the edge stimuli were externally applied to an immobilized finger.
evidence: This claim describes a methodological difference between the current study and previous perceptual studies.

claim: Subtle differences in contact dynamics may contribute to increased acuity during active object manipulation.
source: It is possible that subtle differences in contact dynamics contribute to increased acuity during active object manipulation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms underlying the observed differences.

claim: Some additional information about orientation may be available during the rotation, which could be used to adjust ongoing motor commands generating the rotation.
source: Moreover, although our results indicate that participants rapidly and accurately extract information about orientation prior to object rotation, some additional information about orientation may be available during the rotation, which could be used to adjust ongoing motor commands generating the rotation (see further below).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential online control mechanisms.

claim: In perceptual tasks, participants reported orientation after the stimuli had been removed from the fingertip, requiring reports based on a memorized representation of the tactile stimuli, which decays over time.
source: In the perceptual tasks previously used to assess tactile edge orientation sensitivity, participants reported orientation after the stimuli had been removed from the fingertip. Such reports must be based on a memorized representation of the tactile stimuli, which decays over time (Sinclair and Burton, 1996; Gallace and Spence, 2009).
evidence: This claim describes a methodological feature of previous perceptual studies and its implications, supported by citations on memory decay.

claim: Memory decay was reduced in the current task because the response was initiated very soon after the stimulus is contacted and while it remains in contact with the fingertip.
source: Memory decay was reduced in our task because the response (i.e., dial rotation) was initiated very soon after the stimulus is contacted and while it remains in contact with the fingertip.
evidence: This claim is an inference about how the task design reduces memory demands.

claim: The central processing of sensory information depends on task and context.
source: Another factor that might contribute to differences in tactile edge orientation sensitivity in different situations is that the central processing of sensory information depends on task and context (Engel et al., 2001; Crapse and Sommer, 2008; Schroeder et al., 2010; Gazzaley and Nobre, 2012; Zagha et al., 2013; Manita et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on context-dependent sensory processing.

claim: Visual information can be processed differently in motor and perceptual tasks.
source: For example, it is well established that visual information can be processed differently in motor and perceptual tasks (Bridgeman, 2000; Kravitz et al., 2011; Milner and Goodale, 2006; Rossetti and Pisella, 2002; Weiskrantz, 1996) and that such difference partially reflect the engagement of different cortical processing pathways (Milner and Goodale, 2008; Ungerleider and Haxby, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on visual processing pathways.

claim: The dorsal visual pathway, supporting action, is thought to compute real-time motor commands based on directly viewed object metrics.
source: The dorsal visual pathway, supporting action, is thought to compute real-time motor commands based on directly viewed object metrics, and the ventral visual pathway, supporting perception, is thought to extract lasting and detailed information about objects via memory associations and recognition.
evidence: This claim describes established knowledge about visual processing pathways.

claim: The ventral visual pathway, supporting perception, is thought to extract lasting and detailed information about objects via memory associations and recognition.
source: The dorsal visual pathway, supporting action, is thought to compute real-time motor commands based on directly viewed object metrics, and the ventral visual pathway, supporting perception, is thought to extract lasting and detailed information about objects via memory associations and recognition.
evidence: This claim describes established knowledge about visual processing pathways.

claim: Motor-related signals at different levels of the sensorimotor system can affect virtually all levels of the tactile processing pathway.
source: For the somatosensory system, motor-related signals at different levels of the sensorimotor system can affect virtually all levels of the tactile processing pathway (Zagha et al., 2013; Manita et al., 2015; Canedo, 1997; Fanselow and Nicolelis, 1999; Lee et al., 2008; Seki and Fetz, 2012; Adams et al., 2013) and incoming tactile information can be predictively filtered during action, making it possible for the sensorimotor system to attenuate irrelevant inputs and highlight task-critical information (Chapman, 1994; Bays et al., 2005; Blakemore et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on sensorimotor interactions.

claim: Incoming tactile information can be predictively filtered during action, making it possible for the sensorimotor system to attenuate irrelevant inputs and highlight task-critical information.
source: For the somatosensory system, motor-related signals at different levels of the sensorimotor system can affect virtually all levels of the tactile processing pathway (Zagha et al., 2013; Manita et al., 2015; Canedo, 1997; Fanselow and Nicolelis, 1999; Lee et al., 2008; Seki and Fetz, 2012; Adams et al., 2013) and incoming tactile information can be predictively filtered during action, making it possible for the sensorimotor system to attenuate irrelevant inputs and highlight task-critical information (Chapman, 1994; Bays et al., 2005; Blakemore et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on predictive filtering in sensorimotor control.

claim: Tool use is associated with dynamically remapping of space represented by central multisensory, predominantly tactile neurons.
source: Since our task can be considered a tool-use task, it is also interesting to note that tool use is associated with dynamically remapping of space represented by central multisensory, predominantly tactile neurons (Maravita and Iriki, 2004; Brozzoli et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on tool use and spatial remapping.

claim: The added time between touch and rotation onset in the tactile trials (~130 ms) represents the time actually required to extract and process tactile edge orientation information.
source: Since the rotation movement could be programmed before touch in the visual trials, it seems reasonable to suggest that the added time between touch and rotation onset in the tactile trials (~130 ms) represents the time actually required to extract and process tactile edge orientation information.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on comparison of rotation onset times between visual and tactile conditions.

claim: Fast acquisition and use of tactile information is in agreement with the automaticity by which tactile signals are used in other aspects of object manipulation.
source: Such fast acquisition and use of tactile information is in agreement with the automaticity by which tactile signals are used in other aspects of object manipulation, including mechanisms supporting grasp stability (Johansson and Flanagan, 2009) and target-directed reaching guided by touch (Pruszynski et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to previous research on tactile control of manipulation.

claim: There was no effect of the fidelity of the sensory information (i.e. edge length) on the latency of the triggered action (i.e., the start of rotation).
source: Likewise, as with other action patterns rapidly triggered by tactile events during unfolding manipulation (Pruszynski et al., 2016; Johansson and Westling, 1987), we found no effect of the fidelity of the sensory information (i.e. edge length) on the latency of the triggered action (i.e., the start of rotation).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no effect of edge length on rotation onset time.

claim: In perceptual studies, reaction time measures typically increase when the credibility of the sensory information decreases.
source: This contrasts with typical results of perceptual studies where the reaction time measures typically increase when the credibility of the sensory information decreases (Pins and Bonnet, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous perceptual research.

claim: The important tactile information used in the task was acquired very soon after the edge was initially touched and thus signalled by the dynamic responses in first order tactile neurons when the edge deformed the skin during the contact force increase.
source: These results suggest that the important tactile information used in our task was acquired very soon after the edge was initially touched (Johansson and Birznieks, 2004) and thus signalled by the dynamic responses in first order tactile neurons when the edge deformed the skin during the contact force increase.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on experimental findings about timing and the lack of benefit from longer processing time.

claim: Tactile afferent information available later during the rotation would have been restricted largely to gradually fading responses in some of the slowly adapting tactile neurons.
source: Indeed, tactile afferent information available later during the rotation would have been restricted largely to gradually fading responses in some of the slowly adapting tactile neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of tactile neuron response properties.

claim: The dynamic response of first order tactile neurons seems highly informative for the perception of edge orientation since the duration of stimulation seems to marginally influence performance in psychophysical tests.
source: Interestingly, the dynamic response of first order tactile neurons also seems highly informative for the perception of edge orientation since the duration of stimulation seems to marginally influence performance in psychophysical tests – indenting the fingertip with a 10 mm long bar for 400 ms compared to 100 ms only slightly improved average orientation identification threshold (from 26.6 to 23.4°) (Bensmaia et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous psychophysical study.

claim: Both tasks primarily gauged the accuracy of movement planning before rotation onset, where touch specified the initial orientation of the dial in the tactile task and vision in the visual task.
source: We justify our comparison by the fact that both tasks primarily gauged the accuracy of movement planning before rotation onset, where touch specified the initial orientation of the dial in the tactile task and vision in the visual task.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental design and what the tasks measure.

claim: In both tasks, the information available for possible online control of the pointer's state during rotation was restricted to proprioceptive and/or efference information about the movement of the hand.
source: Since there was no visual feedback during the rotational movement in any of the tasks, in both tasks the information available for possible online control of the pointer's state (position, velocity) was restricted to proprioceptive and/or efference information about the movement of the hand (Desmurget and Grafton, 2000).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental design and supported by citation on motor control.

claim: Tactile signals related to the orientation of the edge would provide information about the pointer's orientation relative to the fingertip rather than information about the pointer's orientation in external space.
source: The fact that the edge was touched during the rotation in the tactile trial did not mean that tactile afferent signals from the fingertip conveyed information about the pointer's state during the rotation. Tactile signals related to the orientation of the edge would provide information about the pointer's orientation relative to the fingertip rather than information about the pointer's orientation in external space.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the reference frame of tactile information during rotation.

claim: The dial offered negligible resistance to rotation due to its very low rotational friction and moment of inertia, limiting skin deformation changes related to rotation of the dial.
source: Because of its very low rotational friction and moment of inertia (see Materials and methods), the dial offered negligible resistance to rotation, limiting skin deformation changes related to rotation of the dial (i.e., no rotational slips and virtually no twist forces impeding the movement occurred in the digit-dial interface during the rotation).
evidence: This claim is based on the physical properties of the apparatus described in the methods.

claim: Signals mainly in slowly adaptive tactile neurons could have helped in the tactile task by facilitating possible proprioceptively based online control by gradually improving the assessment of the orientation of the edge relative to the fingertip during the ongoing movement.
source: However, we cannot fully exclude that signals mainly in slowly adaptive tactile neurons could have helped in the tactile task by facilitating possible proprioceptively based online control by gradually improving the assessment of the orientation of the edge relative to the fingertip during the ongoing movement.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential contributions of slowly adapting neurons.

claim: The actual sensitivity of the tactile apparatus to edge orientation must be better than indicated by the experiment.
source: The actual sensitivity of the tactile apparatus to edge orientation must be better than indicated by our experiment, since our approach, though naturalistic, introduces several sources of information loss in this regard.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the true capabilities of the tactile system given experimental limitations.

claim: Sources of information loss in the experiment include noise related to arm-hand coordination and postural actions, as well as information loss associated with memory decay.
source: This would include noise related to arm-hand coordination and postural actions in our standing participants, as well as information loss associated with memory decay.
evidence: This claim identifies specific sources of variability in the experimental task.

claim: The edge orientation sensitivity revealed in the tactile pointer-alignment task substantially exceeds that predicted by the Shannon-Nyquist sampling theorem if assuming a pixel-like mosaic of tactile innervation determined by the density of relevant first-order tactile neurons in the human fingertips.
source: Yet, the edge orientation sensitivity as revealed in our tactile pointer-alignment task substantially exceeds that predicted by the Shannon-Nyquist sampling theorem if assuming a pixel-like mosaic of tactile innervation determined by the density of relevant first-order tactile neurons in the human fingertips.
evidence: This claim compares experimental results to theoretical predictions based on sampling theory.

claim: With the 4 mm edge, the average alignment error (5.9°) corresponds to a position change of just 0.21 mm at the end of the edge if rotated around its center, which is very small in relation to the ~1 mm average spacing between receptive field centers in human fingertips.
source: For example, with the 4 mm edge the average alignment error (5.9°) corresponds to a position change of just 0.21 mm at the end of the edge if rotated around its center, which is very small in relation to the ~1 mm average spacing between receptive field centers in human fingertips (Johansson and Vallbo, 1979) (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim combines experimental data with known anatomical facts to illustrate hyperacuity.

claim: The ability of humans to perform spatial discrimination finer than that predicted by the average spacing between receptive field centers, termed hyperacuity, has been examined extensively in vision and has also been reported for touch.
source: The ability of humans to perform spatial discrimination finer than that predicted by the average spacing between receptive field centers, termed hyperacuity, has been examined extensively in vision (Westheimer, 2012), but has also been reported for touch (Dodson et al., 1998; Wheat et al., 1995; Loomis, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on hyperacuity in vision and touch.

claim: The currently accepted model supporting tactile hyperacuity centers on the assumption that first-order tactile neurons have simple Gaussian-like sensitivity profiles.
source: The currently accepted model supporting tactile hyperacuity, built largely on neural recordings in monkeys, centers on the assumption that first-order tactile neurons have simple Gaussian-like sensitivity profiles; at the population level, this model proposes that spatial details are resolved by comparing the discharge rates of neurons – generally estimated over hundreds of milliseconds (Khalsa et al., 1998) – with neighbouring receptive fields via an unknown neural interpolation scheme (Friedman et al., 2002; Dodson et al., 1998; Wheat et al., 1995; Saal et al., 2017; Loomis and Collins, 1978).
evidence: This claim describes the prevailing model in the field, supported by citations.

claim: At the population level, the currently accepted model proposes that spatial details are resolved by comparing the discharge rates of neurons with neighbouring receptive fields via an unknown neural interpolation scheme.
source: The currently accepted model supporting tactile hyperacuity, built largely on neural recordings in monkeys, centers on the assumption that first-order tactile neurons have simple Gaussian-like sensitivity profiles; at the population level, this model proposes that spatial details are resolved by comparing the discharge rates of neurons – generally estimated over hundreds of milliseconds (Khalsa et al., 1998) – with neighbouring receptive fields via an unknown neural interpolation scheme (Friedman et al., 2002; Dodson et al., 1998; Wheat et al., 1995; Saal et al., 2017; Loomis and Collins, 1978).
evidence: This claim describes the prevailing model in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The average spacing between subfields is substantially less than the average spacing between receptive field centers.
source: Under our proposed scheme, the degree to which different edge orientations synchronously engage different subsets of neurons determines edge orientation resolution, which would be higher than predicted by the center-to-center spacing of the receptive fields because the average spacing between subfields is substantially less than the average spacing between receptive field centers.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the proposed model of receptive field organization with subfields.

claim: The massive divergence and convergence of first-order neurons in the periphery onto second and higher order neurons in the central nervous system, together with these neurons functioning as efficient coincidence detectors, could allow fast feedforward processing of spatially correlated spiking activity in ensembles of first-order neurons.
source: That is, the massive divergence and convergence of first-order neurons in the periphery onto second and higher order neurons in the central nervous system (Jones, 2000), together with these neurons functioning as efficient coincidence detectors (König et al., 1996; Usrey, 2002), could allow fast feedforward processing of spatially correlated spiking activity in ensembles of first-order neurons (Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014; Johansson and Birznieks, 2004; Johansson and Flanagan, 2009; Jörntell et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is a theoretical proposal supported by citations to previous work on neural connectivity and coincidence detection.

claim: The convergence of inputs from multiple mechanoreceptive transduction sites on individual first-order neurons (yielding subfields) represents an optimal scheme for preserving behaviourally relevant spatial tactile information given the relatively tight space constraints for neurons in the peripheral nerve and dorsal root ganglion as compared to mechanoreceptors in the skin.
source: We believe that the convergence of inputs from multiple mechanoreceptive transduction sites on individual first-order neurons (yielding subfields) represents an optimal scheme for preserving behaviourally relevant spatial tactile information given the relatively tight space constraints for neurons in the peripheral nerve (axons) and dorsal root ganglion (cell bodies) as compared to mechanoreceptors in the skin (Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the evolutionary/functional rationale for the observed neural architecture.

claim: Recent work from the field of compressed sensing shows that randomly sampling a sparse input signal often allows it to be fully reconstructed with fewer measurements than predicted by the Shannon-Nyquist theorem.
source: For example, recent work from the field of compressed sensing shows that randomly sampling a sparse input signal often allows it to be fully reconstructed with fewer measurements than predicted by the Shannon-Nyquist theorem (Candes and Wakin, 2008; Candès et al., 2006), suggesting that heterogeneous connections in the tactile periphery may help overcome sensory processing bottlenecks related to pathway convergence (Candes and Wakin, 2008; Candès et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to work on compressed sensing.

claim: Heterogeneous connections in the tactile periphery may help overcome sensory processing bottlenecks related to pathway convergence.
source: For example, recent work from the field of compressed sensing shows that randomly sampling a sparse input signal often allows it to be fully reconstructed with fewer measurements than predicted by the Shannon-Nyquist theorem (Candes and Wakin, 2008; Candès et al., 2006), suggesting that heterogeneous connections in the tactile periphery may help overcome sensory processing bottlenecks related to pathway convergence (Candes and Wakin, 2008; Candès et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative claim connecting compressed sensing theory to tactile neural architecture.
